subject: english-literature
title: How to Compare: Form, Structure, Language
welcome_lead: Learn the comparative methodology OCR rewards: paired analysis of form, structure, language, voice, and context across two poems.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR Comparative Poetry adventure on methodology: form, structure, language, voice, and context.
final_note: Good comparison is not a list of similarities and differences. It is an argument about how two poems illuminate each other.

concepts.def: OCR comparative essays should integrate two poems throughout, not analyse them sequentially; comparison should be argumentative.
The specific moments — image, line break, rhyme — where two poems can be brought into productive juxtaposition.
Form (sonnet, ode, free verse) and structure (stanza pattern, volta, rhetorical arc) are the first comparative axes.
Word choice and tonal range — Latinate vs Anglo-Saxon, demotic vs elevated; reveal poetic temperament and audience address.
Who speaks, to whom, and how? First-person lyric, dramatic monologue, second-person address all configure reader-poem relations differently.
Historical, biographical, literary context should illuminate the poem, not displace close reading.

walkthroughs.body_html: Weaker comparative essays analyse Poem A in full, then Poem B in full, then offer cursory comparison. Stronger essays integrate: each paragraph holds both poems in tension, organised by analytical category (e.g. handling of address, use of caesura). OCR mark schemes reward sustained comparison at the level of sentence and paragraph. Examiners look for connective phrasing — 'whereas', 'by contrast', 'similarly attenuated' — that signals continuous comparative thought.

If both poems are sonnets, compare the variant: Petrarchan (octave/sestet, ABBAABBA CDECDE) vs Shakespearean (three quatrains + couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG) vs Spenserian (interlocking ABAB BCBC CDCD EE). Note location of volta — line 9 (Petrarchan), line 13 (Shakespearean), or displaced. The same form can be filled with utterly different content, but the form itself constrains and enables. Comparing sonnets compels reflection on how tradition is inhabited differently.

'Sonnet 116' addresses no specified hearer; 'Sonnet 130' addresses none either but constructs an implicit poetic-critical reader. Donne's 'The Sun Rising' addresses the sun; Browning's 'My Last Duchess' addresses a silent envoy. Each address creates different reader positions. Comparison should attend not just to that poems address differently but to what each mode of address enables and forecloses.
